answer:
**≈ 11 g of protein in four boiled egg yolks**

| Source | Protein per yolk | Protein in 4 yolks |
|--------|-------------------|--------------------|
| USDA FoodData Central (large egg) | 2.7 g | 2.7 × 4 ≈ **10.8 g** |
| Egginfo (medium‑size yolk) | 2.5 g | 2.5 × 4 = **10.0 g** |

**How the figure is derived**

- A large boiled egg yolk contains roughly 2.7 g of protein (USDA data).  
- Multiply that by four: 2.7 g × 4 = 10.8 g.  
- If you use the slightly lower figure from Egginfo (2.5 g per yolk), the total comes to 10 g.  

**TL;DR** – Four boiled egg yolks provide about 10–11 grams of protein. If you’re counting protein for a meal, remember that the yolk is the protein‑dense part of the egg, but the white contributes a bit more total protein per whole egg.

Title: Egg yolk nutrition | Egg Recipes – British Lion Eggs
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5
Egg yolks are the nourishing nucleus of the egg and contain nutrients such as essential fatty acids, vitamins, protein and minerals. Egg yolks are also the rich, flavoursome portion of the egg and are often used in recipes to enhance flavours and bind ingredients.

## Egg yolk nutrition information
| Nutrition Information | Per Yolk from Medium Size Egg (58 grams) | Per 100 grams |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| Energy kcals (calories) | 52 | 347 |  
| Energy kJ | 217 | 1437 |  
| Fat (g) | 4.7 | 31.3 |  
| Saturates (g) | 1.3 | 8.8 |  
| Monounsaturates (g) | 1.8 | 12.0 |  
| Polyunsaturates (g) | 0.8 | 5.0 |  
| Carbohydrate (g) | 0.0 | 0.0 |  
| Sugars (g) | 0.0 | 0.0 |  
| Protein (g) | 2.5 | 16.4 |  
| Salt (g) | 0.02 | 0.13 |

## Vitamins and minerals
Egg yolks contain a number of vitamins including B12, B2, A, and folate. Egg yolks are also one of the few foods that naturally contain vitamin D which is essential for healthy bones and teeth. Just like vitamins, minerals are also essential for our bodies to function and contribute to our overall wellbeing. Egg yolks contain many minerals including phosphorus, iodine and selenium.

## Protein
Egg whites are usually associated with high protein levels, but the yolks actually contain more protein than the whites, gram for gram. The average protein content of yolk is 16.4g per 100g, compared to 10.8g in the egg white per 100g.Although good quality protein can be found in the yolk, it is the egg white (albumen) that has the most because there is more white than yolk in each egg.

## Essential fatty acids
Fats are an essential part of any healthy diet, and egg yolks are a good source of polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fats. Egg yolks also contain omega-3 fatty acids which have a number of benefits including contributing to the maintenance of normal heart and brain function.
Although egg yolks are nutritious, don’t forget about the whites! They have their own benefits to offer and therefore should be enjoyed together with the yolk for complete nutrition – as a source of high quality protein. Find out more about egg white nutrition.

opened.anchor: Hard-Boiled Egg Nutrition Facts: Calories, Protein and More
opened.information:
Source: https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/boiled-egg-nutrition
Title: Hard-Boiled Egg Nutrition Facts: Calories, Protein and More
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Eggs are a protein and nutrient powerhouse. They are low in calories, can be added to many dishes, and can be prepared in numerous ways. They do contain cholesterol, but this is not harmful to most people.
**One way to enjoy eggs is to hard-boil them**. Hard-boiled eggs make great salad toppings and can be eaten with salt and pepper.
Here is everything you need to know about hard-boiled eggs.
Hard-boiled eggs are loaded with **nutrients**, **protein**, and **healthy****fats**. One large hard-boiled egg (50 grams) provides:
*   Calories: 77.5 kcal  
*   Carbs: .56 g  
*   Total fat: 5.3 g  
*   Saturated fat: 1.64 g  
*   Monounsaturated fat: 2.04 g  
*   Cholesterol: 186 mg  
*   Protein: 6.3 g  
*   Vitamin A: 74.5 mcg RAE  
*   Vitamin B2 (riboflavin): 0.257 mg  
*   Vitamin B12 (cobalamin): 0.555 µg  
*   Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid): 0.7 mg  
*   Phosphorus: 86 mg  
*   Selenium: 15.4 µg
For all the nutrients eggs have to offer, they are **a fairly low calorie food**. Hard-boiled eggs provide only **77.5 calories, 5.3 grams of fat, and a very small amount of carbs**.
They’re also a very good source of lean **protein**, at about **6 grams per egg**. Furthermore, eggs pack a **complete range of amino acids**, which means they are a complete protein source.
Hard-boiled eggs also offer various important nutrients, including **vitamin D**, **zinc**, **calcium**, and all of the **B vitamins**. They’re a particularly good source of **riboflavin** (vitamin B2) and vitamin B12.
Many of the nutrients in an egg are found exclusively in the yolk, whereas the egg white contains primarily protein.

> **Summary**  
> Hard-boiled eggs are low in calories and rich in many important vitamins, minerals and nutrients. While the yolk provides nutrients, fat and protein, the white is almost exclusively protein.
**Protein is vital for many components of your health**, including building muscle and bones and producing hormones and enzymes. **Eggs provide about 6 grams of high quality protein**. In fact, eggs are one of the best sources of protein you can eat.
This is due to their complete protein profile — **eggs contain all nine essential amino acids**.
One common misconception is that the protein is found only in the egg white. However, **almost half of an egg’s protein content comes from the yolk**.
Consume the entire egg, yolk and white, to get the most benefit from the protein and nutrients it contains.
> **Summary**  
> Eggs are an excellent source of protein. They contain all nine essential amino acids, and both the white and yolk contain this important nutrient.
Over the years, eggs have gotten a bad reputation due to their high cholesterol content. **It’s true that eggs are packed with cholesterol**. One large hard-boiled egg provides **186 mg of cholesterol**. However, recent research shows that **dietary cholesterol has very little effect on blood cholesterol,** and the Dietary Guidelines no longer have a daily recommended amount of cholesterol.
For most people, dietary cholesterol is not associated with heart disease risk and **does not increase total cholesterol or “bad” LDL cholesterol levels**.
In fact, **egg consumption may improve “good” HDL cholesterol**. Ultimately, more research is needed on the link between egg consumption and heart disease risk in people with diabetes.
> **Summary**  
> Though hard-boiled eggs are high in cholesterol, studies show that dietary cholesterol does not negatively impact blood cholesterol in most people. In fact, eggs have been found to improve cholesterol profiles by increasing “good” HDL cholesterol.
Eggs provide important essential nutrients and antioxidants that support brain and eye health.

### Choline
**Choline is an essential nutrient for many critical processes** in your body. Your body does produce some choline on its own, but not in large quantities. Therefore, **you must get choline from your diet in order to avoid deficiency**.
Yet, **most Americans aren’t consuming enough**.
**Choline is crucial for maintaining a healthy nervous system**, as it helps **produce****acetylcholine**, a neurotransmitter involved in memory and learning. Choline is important across your lifespan. It promotes **fetal brain and memory development**, as well as **cognitive****function** in older adults.
**It’s also vital during pregnancy**, as adequate choline levels may decrease the risk of neural tube defects in the fetus.
**Choline is found in the yolk** — one, large, hard-boiled egg contains **147 mg of choline**, which is 27% of the Daily Value for choline. In fact, eggs are one of the most concentrated sources of choline in the American diet.

### Lutein and Zeaxanthin
**Lutein** and **zeaxanthin** are two **antioxidants best known for their role in eye health**. They combat harmful, oxygen-induced free radicals that can accumulate in your eyes.
Research suggests that Lutein and zeaxanthin have been shown to slow the formation of cataracts and protect against age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
They may even protect your eyes from detrimental blue light. Egg yolks are an excellent source of these two carotenoids. Furthermore, due to the yolk’s fat profile, your body appears to absorb the lutein and zeaxanthin very well.
> **Summary**  
> Egg yolks are an excellent source of choline, which is essential for brain health and development. They’re also rich in lutein and zeaxanthin, antioxidants that promote eye health.
Hard-boiled eggs are made by placing unshelled eggs in a saucepan filled with cold water, then boiling until the yolk solidifies. They’re cooked without any additional butter or oil. On the other hand, fried eggs require supplemental butter or oil, which contribute additional calories and fat.
**Other than the fat and calorie content, hard-boiled and fried eggs have very similar vitamin and mineral profiles. They don’t differ in their amount of protein and nutrients.**
> **Summary**  
> While hard-boiled eggs are prepared without further ingredients, fried eggs require additional butter or oil — which make them higher in calories. However, fried and boiled eggs are very similar from a micronutrient standpoint.
**Hard-boiled eggs are a low calorie, nutrient-dense food**. They’re an excellent source of **high****quality****protein** and rich in **B vitamins**, **selenium** (28% DV), **vitamin****A** (8% DV), and other important nutrients and antioxidants like choline, lutein, and zeaxanthin.
Though high in cholesterol, eggs don’t appear to increase heart disease risk in most people. Hard-boiled eggs are prepared without additional oil or butter, so they’re lower in calories and fat than fried eggs.
They may just be one of the easiest and most nutritious additions to your diet.

# Here's How Much Protein You Really Get from 1 Egg
## Average Protein Content Per Egg
On average, there are 5-8 grams of protein in an egg, depending on its size. Here’s how much protein you’ll find in different sizes of eggs:
*   **Small:**5 grams (g) protein  
*   **Medium:**6 g protein  
*   **Large:**6 g protein  
*   **Extra large:**7 g protein  
*   **Jumbo:**8 g protein
Eggs are a complete source of protein. This means they offer all nine essential amino acids your body cannot produce on its own and needs to get through diet. This high-quality protein is important for:
*   Bone health  
*   Muscle health  
*   Immune health  
*   Vision health  
*   Skin and hair health  
*   Hormone production

## Egg Yolk vs. White
Whole eggs have two parts: the white and the yolk. Both have protein, but in different amounts. They also give your body different nutrients. Here’s how they compare.

# Here's How Much Protein You Really Get from 1 Egg
## Egg Yolk vs. White
### Egg Yolk
A large egg yolk has about 2.7 grams of protein. It has slightly less protein than egg white but gives more nutrients, like vitamins A, D, E, and K, plus several B vitamins. The egg yolk also provides healthy fats, iron, zinc, and choline, an important nutrient for brain health.

# Here's How Much Protein You Really Get from 1 Egg
## Egg Yolk vs. White
### Egg White
Egg whites have more protein than the yolk, with about 3.6 grams per large egg white. They’re also low in calories and nearly fat-free, making them a good option if you want to boost your protein without adding many calories. Egg whites are also a source of vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid).

## Tips for Eating Eggs
Whether you eat them boiled as a snack or scrambled for breakfast, eggs are a convenient way to boost your protein intake.
Research shows that eggs can help increase fullness, reduce body fat, and support muscle growth. In one 2020 study, participants who ate eggs for breakfast consumed fewer calories later in the day.
In another 2020 study, people who ate two eggs most days of the week maintained higher vitamin D levels compared to those who ate cereal. This is important because many people don’t get enough vitamin D, a nutrient that supports bone health and immunity.
Here are some tips on how to use eggs to boost the protein content of your meals:
*   Pair scrambled eggs or an omelet for breakfast with a whole-grain muffin  
*   Add half a cup of cottage cheese to two scrambled eggs for a total of 23 grams of protein  
*   Slice a boiled egg onto your salad  
*   Keep hard-boiled eggs in the fridge for an easy, portable snack  
*   Add egg whites to baked oatmeal to boost protein

*   Make egg bites or mini frittatas ahead of time for busy days

# Here's How Much Protein You Really Get from 1 Egg
## Average Protein Content Per Egg
On average, there are 5-8 grams of protein in an egg, depending on its size. Here’s how much protein you’ll find in different sizes of eggs:
*   **Small:**5 grams (g) protein  
*   **Medium:**6 g protein  
*   **Large:**6 g protein  
*   **Extra large:**7 g protein  
*   **Jumbo:**8 g protein
Eggs are a complete source of protein. This means they offer all nine essential amino acids your body cannot produce on its own and needs to get through diet. This high-quality protein is important for:
*   Bone health  
*   Muscle health  
*   Immune health  
*   Vision health  
*   Skin and hair health  
*   Hormone production

# Here's How Much Protein You Really Get from 1 Egg
## Egg Yolk vs. White
### Egg Yolk
A large egg yolk has about 2.7 grams of protein. It has slightly less protein than egg white but gives more nutrients, like vitamins A, D, E, and K, plus several B vitamins. The egg yolk also provides healthy fats, iron, zinc, and choline, an important nutrient for brain health.

# Here's How Much Protein You Really Get from 1 Egg
## Egg Yolk vs. White
### Egg White
Egg whites have more protein than the yolk, with about 3.6 grams per large egg white. They’re also low in calories and nearly fat-free, making them a good option if you want to boost your protein without adding many calories. Egg whites are also a source of vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid).

# Here's How Much Protein You Really Get from 1 Egg
## Tips for Eating Eggs
Whether you eat them boiled as a snack or scrambled for breakfast, eggs are a convenient way to boost your protein intake.
Research shows that eggs can help increase fullness, reduce body fat, and support muscle growth. In one 2020 study, participants who ate eggs for breakfast consumed fewer calories later in the day.
In another 2020 study, people who ate two eggs most days of the week maintained higher vitamin D levels compared to those who ate cereal. This is important because many people don’t get enough vitamin D, a nutrient that supports bone health and immunity.
Here are some tips on how to use eggs to boost the protein content of your meals:
*   Pair scrambled eggs or an omelet for breakfast with a whole-grain muffin  
*   Add half a cup of cottage cheese to two scrambled eggs for a total of 23 grams of protein  
*   Slice a boiled egg onto your salad  
*   Keep hard-boiled eggs in the fridge for an easy, portable snack  
*   Add egg whites to baked oatmeal to boost protein

*   Make egg bites or mini frittatas ahead of time for busy days

## Vitamins and minerals
Egg yolks contain a number of vitamins including B12, B2, A, and folate. Egg yolks are also one of the few foods that naturally contain vitamin D which is essential for healthy bones and teeth. Just like vitamins, minerals are also essential for our bodies to function and contribute to our overall wellbeing. Egg yolks contain many minerals including phosphorus, iodine and selenium.
texts.3:
## Protein
Egg whites are usually associated with high protein levels, but the yolks actually contain more protein than the whites, gram for gram. The average protein content of yolk is 16.4g per 100g, compared to 10.8g in the egg white per 100g.Although good quality protein can be found in the yolk, it is the egg white (albumen) that has the most because there is more white than yolk in each egg.
texts.4:
## Essential fatty acids
Fats are an essential part of any healthy diet, and egg yolks are a good source of polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fats. Egg yolks also contain omega-3 fatty acids which have a number of benefits including contributing to the maintenance of normal heart and brain function.
Although egg yolks are nutritious, don’t forget about the whites! They have their own benefits to offer and therefore should be enjoyed together with the yolk for complete nutrition – as a source of high quality protein. Find out more about egg white nutrition.

Eggs are a protein and nutrient powerhouse. They are low in calories, can be added to many dishes, and can be prepared in numerous ways. They do contain cholesterol, but this is not harmful to most people.
**One way to enjoy eggs is to hard-boil them**. Hard-boiled eggs make great salad toppings and can be eaten with salt and pepper.
Here is everything you need to know about hard-boiled eggs.
Hard-boiled eggs are loaded with **nutrients**, **protein**, and **healthy****fats**. One large hard-boiled egg (50 grams) provides:
*   Calories: 77.5 kcal  
*   Carbs: .56 g  
*   Total fat: 5.3 g  
*   Saturated fat: 1.64 g  
*   Monounsaturated fat: 2.04 g  
*   Cholesterol: 186 mg  
*   Protein: 6.3 g  
*   Vitamin A: 74.5 mcg RAE  
*   Vitamin B2 (riboflavin): 0.257 mg  
*   Vitamin B12 (cobalamin): 0.555 µg  
*   Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid): 0.7 mg  
*   Phosphorus: 86 mg  
*   Selenium: 15.4 µg
For all the nutrients eggs have to offer, they are **a fairly low calorie food**. Hard-boiled eggs provide only **77.5 calories, 5.3 grams of fat, and a very small amount of carbs**.
They’re also a very good source of lean **protein**, at about **6 grams per egg**. Furthermore, eggs pack a **complete range of amino acids**, which means they are a complete protein source.
Hard-boiled eggs also offer various important nutrients, including **vitamin D**, **zinc**, **calcium**, and all of the **B vitamins**. They’re a particularly good source of **riboflavin** (vitamin B2) and vitamin B12.
Many of the nutrients in an egg are found exclusively in the yolk, whereas the egg white contains primarily protein.
texts.1:
> **Summary**  
> Hard-boiled eggs are low in calories and rich in many important vitamins, minerals and nutrients. While the yolk provides nutrients, fat and protein, the white is almost exclusively protein.
**Protein is vital for many components of your health**, including building muscle and bones and producing hormones and enzymes. **Eggs provide about 6 grams of high quality protein**. In fact, eggs are one of the best sources of protein you can eat.
This is due to their complete protein profile — **eggs contain all nine essential amino acids**.
One common misconception is that the protein is found only in the egg white. However, **almost half of an egg’s protein content comes from the yolk**.
Consume the entire egg, yolk and white, to get the most benefit from the protein and nutrients it contains.
> **Summary**  
> Eggs are an excellent source of protein. They contain all nine essential amino acids, and both the white and yolk contain this important nutrient.
Over the years, eggs have gotten a bad reputation due to their high cholesterol content. **It’s true that eggs are packed with cholesterol**. One large hard-boiled egg provides **186 mg of cholesterol**. However, recent research shows that **dietary cholesterol has very little effect on blood cholesterol,** and the Dietary Guidelines no longer have a daily recommended amount of cholesterol.
For most people, dietary cholesterol is not associated with heart disease risk and **does not increase total cholesterol or “bad” LDL cholesterol levels**.
In fact, **egg consumption may improve “good” HDL cholesterol**. Ultimately, more research is needed on the link between egg consumption and heart disease risk in people with diabetes.
> **Summary**  
> Though hard-boiled eggs are high in cholesterol, studies show that dietary cholesterol does not negatively impact blood cholesterol in most people. In fact, eggs have been found to improve cholesterol profiles by increasing “good” HDL cholesterol.
Eggs provide important essential nutrients and antioxidants that support brain and eye health.
texts.2:
### Choline
**Choline is an essential nutrient for many critical processes** in your body. Your body does produce some choline on its own, but not in large quantities. Therefore, **you must get choline from your diet in order to avoid deficiency**.
Yet, **most Americans aren’t consuming enough**.
**Choline is crucial for maintaining a healthy nervous system**, as it helps **produce****acetylcholine**, a neurotransmitter involved in memory and learning. Choline is important across your lifespan. It promotes **fetal brain and memory development**, as well as **cognitive****function** in older adults.
**It’s also vital during pregnancy**, as adequate choline levels may decrease the risk of neural tube defects in the fetus.
**Choline is found in the yolk** — one, large, hard-boiled egg contains **147 mg of choline**, which is 27% of the Daily Value for choline. In fact, eggs are one of the most concentrated sources of choline in the American diet.
texts.3:
### Lutein and Zeaxanthin
**Lutein** and **zeaxanthin** are two **antioxidants best known for their role in eye health**. They combat harmful, oxygen-induced free radicals that can accumulate in your eyes.
Research suggests that Lutein and zeaxanthin have been shown to slow the formation of cataracts and protect against age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
They may even protect your eyes from detrimental blue light. Egg yolks are an excellent source of these two carotenoids. Furthermore, due to the yolk’s fat profile, your body appears to absorb the lutein and zeaxanthin very well.
> **Summary**  
> Egg yolks are an excellent source of choline, which is essential for brain health and development. They’re also rich in lutein and zeaxanthin, antioxidants that promote eye health.
Hard-boiled eggs are made by placing unshelled eggs in a saucepan filled with cold water, then boiling until the yolk solidifies. They’re cooked without any additional butter or oil. On the other hand, fried eggs require supplemental butter or oil, which contribute additional calories and fat.
**Other than the fat and calorie content, hard-boiled and fried eggs have very similar vitamin and mineral profiles. They don’t differ in their amount of protein and nutrients.**
> **Summary**  
> While hard-boiled eggs are prepared without further ingredients, fried eggs require additional butter or oil — which make them higher in calories. However, fried and boiled eggs are very similar from a micronutrient standpoint.
**Hard-boiled eggs are a low calorie, nutrient-dense food**. They’re an excellent source of **high****quality****protein** and rich in **B vitamins**, **selenium** (28% DV), **vitamin****A** (8% DV), and other important nutrients and antioxidants like choline, lutein, and zeaxanthin.
Though high in cholesterol, eggs don’t appear to increase heart disease risk in most people. Hard-boiled eggs are prepared without additional oil or butter, so they’re lower in calories and fat than fried eggs.
They may just be one of the easiest and most nutritious additions to your diet.

# Here's How Much Protein You Really Get from 1 Egg
## Average Protein Content Per Egg
On average, there are 5-8 grams of protein in an egg, depending on its size. Here’s how much protein you’ll find in different sizes of eggs:
*   **Small:**5 grams (g) protein  
*   **Medium:**6 g protein  
*   **Large:**6 g protein  
*   **Extra large:**7 g protein  
*   **Jumbo:**8 g protein

*   Bone health  
*   Muscle health  
*   Immune health  
*   Vision health

Egg yolks are the nourishing nucleus of the egg and contain nutrients such as essential fatty acids, vitamins, protein and minerals. Egg yolks are also the rich, flavoursome portion of the egg and are often used in recipes to enhance flavours and bind ingredients.

## Egg yolk nutrition information
| Nutrition Information | Per Yolk from Medium Size Egg (58 grams) | Per 100 grams |

## Vitamins and minerals
Egg yolks contain a number of vitamins including B12, B2, A, and folate. Egg yolks are also one of the few foods that naturally contain vitamin D which is essential for healthy bones and teeth. Just like vitamins, minerals are also essential for our bodies to function and contribute to our overall wellbeing. Egg yolks contain many minerals including phosphorus, iodine and selenium.

## Protein
Egg whites are usually associated with high protein levels, but the yolks actually contain more protein than the whites, gram for gram. The average protein content of yolk is 16.4g per 100g, compared to 10.8g in the egg white per 100g.Although good quality protein can be found in the yolk, it is the egg white (albumen) that has the most because there is more white than yolk in each egg.

## Essential fatty acids
Fats are an essential part of any healthy diet, and egg yolks are a good source of polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fats. Egg yolks also contain omega-3 fatty acids which have a number of benefits including contributing to the maintenance of normal heart and brain function.
Although egg yolks are nutritious, don’t forget about the whites! They have their own benefits to offer and therefore should be enjoyed together with the yolk for complete nutrition – as a source of high quality protein. Find out more about egg white nutrition.

Title: Hard-Boiled Egg Nutrition Facts: Calories, Protein and More
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Eggs are a protein and nutrient powerhouse. They are low in calories, can be added to many dishes, and can be prepared in numerous ways. They do contain cholesterol, but this is not harmful to most people.
**One way to enjoy eggs is to hard-boil them**. Hard-boiled eggs make great salad toppings and can be eaten with salt and pepper.
Here is everything you need to know about hard-boiled eggs.
Hard-boiled eggs are loaded with **nutrients**, **protein**, and **healthy****fats**. One large hard-boiled egg (50 grams) provides:
*   Calories: 77.5 kcal  
*   Carbs: .56 g  
*   Total fat: 5.3 g  
*   Saturated fat: 1.64 g  
*   Monounsaturated fat: 2.04 g  
*   Cholesterol: 186 mg  
*   Protein: 6.3 g  
*   Vitamin A: 74.5 mcg RAE  
*   Vitamin B2 (riboflavin): 0.257 mg  
*   Vitamin B12 (cobalamin): 0.555 µg  
*   Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid): 0.7 mg  
*   Phosphorus: 86 mg  
*   Selenium: 15.4 µg
For all the nutrients eggs have to offer, they are **a fairly low calorie food**. Hard-boiled eggs provide only **77.5 calories, 5.3 grams of fat, and a very small amount of carbs**.
They’re also a very good source of lean **protein**, at about **6 grams per egg**. Furthermore, eggs pack a **complete range of amino acids**, which means they are a complete protein source.
Hard-boiled eggs also offer various important nutrients, including **vitamin D**, **zinc**, **calcium**, and all of the **B vitamins**. They’re a particularly good source of **riboflavin** (vitamin B2) and vitamin B12.
Many of the nutrients in an egg are found exclusively in the yolk, whereas the egg white contains primarily protein.

> **Summary**  
> Hard-boiled eggs are low in calories and rich in many important vitamins, minerals and nutrients. While the yolk provides nutrients, fat and protein, the white is almost exclusively protein.
**Protein is vital for many components of your health**, including building muscle and bones and producing hormones and enzymes. **Eggs provide about 6 grams of high quality protein**. In fact, eggs are one of the best sources of protein you can eat.
This is due to their complete protein profile — **eggs contain all nine essential amino acids**.
One common misconception is that the protein is found only in the egg white. However, **almost half of an egg’s protein content comes from the yolk**.
Consume the entire egg, yolk and white, to get the most benefit from the protein and nutrients it contains.
> **Summary**  
> Eggs are an excellent source of protein. They contain all nine essential amino acids, and both the white and yolk contain this important nutrient.
Over the years, eggs have gotten a bad reputation due to their high cholesterol content. **It’s true that eggs are packed with cholesterol**. One large hard-boiled egg provides **186 mg of cholesterol**. However, recent research shows that **dietary cholesterol has very little effect on blood cholesterol,** and the Dietary Guidelines no longer have a daily recommended amount of cholesterol.
For most people, dietary cholesterol is not associated with heart disease risk and **does not increase total cholesterol or “bad” LDL cholesterol levels**.
In fact, **egg consumption may improve “good” HDL cholesterol**. Ultimately, more research is needed on the link between egg consumption and heart disease risk in people with diabetes.
> **Summary**  
> Though hard-boiled eggs are high in cholesterol, studies show that dietary cholesterol does not negatively impact blood cholesterol in most people. In fact, eggs have been found to improve cholesterol profiles by increasing “good” HDL cholesterol.
Eggs provide important essential nutrients and antioxidants that support brain and eye health.

### Choline
**Choline is an essential nutrient for many critical processes** in your body. Your body does produce some choline on its own, but not in large quantities. Therefore, **you must get choline from your diet in order to avoid deficiency**.
Yet, **most Americans aren’t consuming enough**.
**Choline is crucial for maintaining a healthy nervous system**, as it helps **produce****acetylcholine**, a neurotransmitter involved in memory and learning. Choline is important across your lifespan. It promotes **fetal brain and memory development**, as well as **cognitive****function** in older adults.
**It’s also vital during pregnancy**, as adequate choline levels may decrease the risk of neural tube defects in the fetus.
**Choline is found in the yolk** — one, large, hard-boiled egg contains **147 mg of choline**, which is 27% of the Daily Value for choline. In fact, eggs are one of the most concentrated sources of choline in the American diet.

### Lutein and Zeaxanthin
**Lutein** and **zeaxanthin** are two **antioxidants best known for their role in eye health**. They combat harmful, oxygen-induced free radicals that can accumulate in your eyes.
Research suggests that Lutein and zeaxanthin have been shown to slow the formation of cataracts and protect against age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
They may even protect your eyes from detrimental blue light. Egg yolks are an excellent source of these two carotenoids. Furthermore, due to the yolk’s fat profile, your body appears to absorb the lutein and zeaxanthin very well.
> **Summary**  
> Egg yolks are an excellent source of choline, which is essential for brain health and development. They’re also rich in lutein and zeaxanthin, antioxidants that promote eye health.
Hard-boiled eggs are made by placing unshelled eggs in a saucepan filled with cold water, then boiling until the yolk solidifies. They’re cooked without any additional butter or oil. On the other hand, fried eggs require supplemental butter or oil, which contribute additional calories and fat.
**Other than the fat and calorie content, hard-boiled and fried eggs have very similar vitamin and mineral profiles. They don’t differ in their amount of protein and nutrients.**
> **Summary**  
> While hard-boiled eggs are prepared without further ingredients, fried eggs require additional butter or oil — which make them higher in calories. However, fried and boiled eggs are very similar from a micronutrient standpoint.
**Hard-boiled eggs are a low calorie, nutrient-dense food**. They’re an excellent source of **high****quality****protein** and rich in **B vitamins**, **selenium** (28% DV), **vitamin****A** (8% DV), and other important nutrients and antioxidants like choline, lutein, and zeaxanthin.
Though high in cholesterol, eggs don’t appear to increase heart disease risk in most people. Hard-boiled eggs are prepared without additional oil or butter, so they’re lower in calories and fat than fried eggs.
They may just be one of the easiest and most nutritious additions to your diet.

## What Makes Egg Protein So Effective?
Before getting into the numbers, it helps to understand why egg protein stands apart from other sources.
Protein quality depends on two main factors: amino acid composition and digestibility. Eggs deliver on both.
**Amino acid profile:** Eggs contain all nine essential amino acids, the ones your body cannot produce on its own and must get from food. This makes eggs a complete protein source. Many plant-based proteins, such as beans or wheat, are incomplete, meaning they lack one or more essential amino acids.
**Digestibility:** The body can absorb and use approximately 95% of the protein in eggs, according to the International Egg Foundation. That absorption rate is higher than most other protein sources, including beef and cow’s milk.
**Benchmark status:** Researchers have historically used eggs as the reference standard, a score of 100, when assessing the protein quality of other foods using the biological value (BV) scale. Few other foods match that benchmark.

## How Many Grams of Protein Are in an Egg?
A single large egg contains **6.3 grams of protein**, according to USDA data compiled by the Iowa Egg Council. That protein is distributed between the white and the yolk, though not evenly.
Here’s the full breakdown per large egg:
| Component | Protein (g) | Calories | Total Fat (g) | Cholesterol (mg) |  
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |  
| **Whole Egg** | 6.3 | 72 | 4.8 | 186 |  
| **Egg White** | 3.6 | 17 | 0.06 | 0 |  
| **Egg Yolk** | 2.7 | 55 | 4.5 | 184 |
The white contributes the majority of the protein in an egg, about 57% of the total. The yolk provides the remaining 43%.

## Protein Concentration: White vs. Yolk Per 100g
The per-egg figures above tell only part of the story. On a gram-for-gram (per 100g) basis, the yolk is actually the more protein-dense component.
| Component | Protein per 100g |  
| --- | --- |  
| **Egg White** | 10.8g |  
| **Egg Yolk** | 16.4g |
The yolk contains more protein by concentration. However, because there is significantly more white than yolk in each egg by volume, the white delivers more total protein per egg. Both figures matter depending on your goal, whether you’re cooking with separated components or eating whole eggs.

## What’s in an Egg White? Protein, Nutrition & Benefits
The egg white, also called albumen, is the clear liquid that surrounds the yolk. It contains the majority of the egg’s protein with almost no fat.
**Egg white nutrition facts (per large egg):**
*   Protein: 3.6g  
*   Calories: 17  
*   Total fat: less than 0.08g  
*   Cholesterol: 0mg  
*   Selenium: 6.6 mcg
The egg white’s near-zero fat content makes it a go-to protein source for people who are managing calorie intake or reducing dietary fat. It’s also cholesterol-free, which matters for individuals who have been advised to monitor their dietary cholesterol intake.
The tradeoff: egg whites contain very little in the way of vitamins and minerals. Fat-soluble vitamins like A, D, E, and K are absent from the white entirely. Smaller amounts of B vitamins, riboflavin, B12, and folate, are present, but in much lower quantities than in the yolk.
**Best for:** People counting calories, reducing fat intake, or managing cholesterol while still hitting protein targets.

## What’s in an Egg Yolk? Protein, Nutrition & Benefits
The yolk is the yellow center of the egg. It carries a smaller amount of total protein per egg than the white, but it is far richer in micronutrients.
**Egg yolk nutrition facts (per large egg):**
*   Protein: 2.7g  
*   Calories: 55  
*   Total fat: 4.5g (including monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats)  
*   Cholesterol: 184mg (210mg in some USDA data sets)  
*   Selenium: 9.5 mcg  
*   Choline: 116mg
All of the egg’s fat-soluble vitamins, A, D, E, and K, are found exclusively in the egg yolk. The yolk also provides the bulk of the egg’s choline (a nutrient essential for brain function), as well as B vitamins including B12, folate, and riboflavin. Minerals like phosphorus, iron, zinc, and calcium are similarly concentrated in the yolk.
On the fat side: the yolk’s fat is primarily monounsaturated and polyunsaturated, including omega-3 fatty acids. These fats support normal brain function and help maintain healthy cholesterol levels. Research published in the American College of Cardiology suggests that regular consumption of two eggs per day does not negatively affect a person’s lipid profile in healthy individuals.
**Best for:** People seeking complete nutrition, broader vitamin and mineral intake, and the benefits of healthy dietary fats alongside their protein.

## Whole Egg vs. Egg White vs. Egg Yolk: Full Nutritional Comparison
The table below compares the full nutritional profile of each egg component using USDA data from the Iowa Egg Council.
| Nutrient | Whole Egg | Egg White | Egg Yolk |  
| --- | --- | --- | --- |  
| Calories | 72 | 17 | 55 |  
| Protein (g) | 6.3 | 3.6 | 2.7 |  
| Total Fat (g) | 4.8 | 0.06 | 4.5 |  
| Carbohydrates (g) | 0.36 | 0.24 | 0.61 |  
| Cholesterol (mg) | 186 | 0 | 184 |  
| Choline (mg) | 126 | 0.4 | 116 |  
| Vitamin A (IU) | 270 | 0 | 245 |  
| Vitamin D (IU) | 41 | 0 | 37 |  
| Vitamin B12 (mcg) | 0.45 | 0.03 | 0.33 |  
| Selenium (mg) | 15.4 | 6.6 | 9.5 |  
| Iron (mg) | 0.88 | 0.03 | 0.46 |  
| Phosphorus (mg) | 99 | 5 | 66 |
**The whole egg provides the most comprehensive nutritional profile.**It combines the protein volume of the white with the vitamin, mineral, and healthy fat content of the yolk, making it the most complete single-food protein option available.

## Which Egg Option Is Right for You?
The right answer depends on your dietary goal.
**Choose egg whites if:**
*   You are minimizing calorie or fat intake  
*   You need a lean, low-cholesterol protein source  
*   You are eating multiple eggs and want to reduce overall fat consumption
**Choose whole eggs if:**
*   You want the most nutritionally complete option  
*   You are not under specific restrictions for cholesterol or fat  
*   You want to maximize vitamins, minerals, and choline alongside protein
**Use the yolk separately if:**
*   You are adding richness, fat-soluble vitamins, or choline to a dish  
*   You are cooking or baking where the yolk serves a functional role
For most healthy adults, eating whole eggs provides the best return on nutritional investment. The yolk’s nutrients, especially choline, vitamin D, and B12, are difficult to replace from other common food sources.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How much protein is in one egg?
One large egg contains 6.3 grams of protein, according to USDA data. This is split between the egg white (3.6g) and the egg yolk (2.7g). The exact amount can vary slightly depending on the size of the egg, medium eggs contain slightly less, while extra-large and jumbo eggs contain slightly more.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many grams of protein are in an egg white only?
One large egg white contains approximately 3.6 grams of protein, 17 calories, and less than 0.08 grams of fat. Egg whites are cholesterol-free and provide a lean, low-calorie protein option.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Does the egg yolk have more protein than the white?
Not per egg, but yes per 100 grams. The egg yolk contains 16.4g of protein per 100g, compared to 10.8g per 100g in the egg white. However, because each egg contains more white than yolk by volume, the white delivers more total protein per egg (3.6g vs. 2.7g).

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How much protein is in two eggs?
Two large eggs provide approximately 12.6 grams of protein, based on the USDA figure of 6.3g per large egg. Two eggs also deliver a full spectrum of vitamins, minerals, and healthy fats, making them a nutritionally complete protein source for most meals.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Is egg protein a complete protein?
Yes. Eggs are a complete protein source, meaning they contain all nine essential amino acids that the body cannot produce on its own. The body absorbs and uses approximately 95% of egg protein, according to the International Egg Foundation, a higher digestibility rate than most other protein sources.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many eggs per day is a healthy amount?
For most healthy adults, research suggests that consuming up to two eggs per day does not negatively impact cholesterol or lipid levels, according to data cited by A Healthier Michigan from the American College of Cardiology. Individuals with coronary artery disease or specific cholesterol concerns should follow guidance from their healthcare provider, as the Mayo Clinic recommends limiting dietary cholesterol in those cases.

## Why Quality Eggs Are the Starting Point
Protein numbers only reflect what’s in the egg. The quality of that egg, from shell integrity to yolk nutrient density, depends on where it comes from and how it was produced.
Eggs from hens raised in healthy conditions and fed quality feed tend to have better nutritional profiles. Certifications like USDA Organic, Certified Humane, and Cage Free (UEP Certified) are reliable indicators of production standards that support both animal welfare and egg quality.

## What Makes Egg Protein So Effective?
Before getting into the numbers, it helps to understand why egg protein stands apart from other sources.
Protein quality depends on two main factors: amino acid composition and digestibility. Eggs deliver on both.
**Amino acid profile:** Eggs contain all nine essential amino acids, the ones your body cannot produce on its own and must get from food. This makes eggs a complete protein source. Many plant-based proteins, such as beans or wheat, are incomplete, meaning they lack one or more essential amino acids.
**Digestibility:** The body can absorb and use approximately 95% of the protein in eggs, according to the International Egg Foundation. That absorption rate is higher than most other protein sources, including beef and cow’s milk.
**Benchmark status:** Researchers have historically used eggs as the reference standard, a score of 100, when assessing the protein quality of other foods using the biological value (BV) scale. Few other foods match that benchmark.

## How Many Grams of Protein Are in an Egg?
A single large egg contains **6.3 grams of protein**, according to USDA data compiled by the Iowa Egg Council. That protein is distributed between the white and the yolk, though not evenly.
Here’s the full breakdown per large egg:
| Component | Protein (g) | Calories | Total Fat (g) | Cholesterol (mg) |  
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |  
| **Whole Egg** | 6.3 | 72 | 4.8 | 186 |  
| **Egg White** | 3.6 | 17 | 0.06 | 0 |  
| **Egg Yolk** | 2.7 | 55 | 4.5 | 184 |
The white contributes the majority of the protein in an egg, about 57% of the total. The yolk provides the remaining 43%.
texts.2:
## Protein Concentration: White vs. Yolk Per 100g
The per-egg figures above tell only part of the story. On a gram-for-gram (per 100g) basis, the yolk is actually the more protein-dense component.
| Component | Protein per 100g |  
| --- | --- |  
| **Egg White** | 10.8g |  
| **Egg Yolk** | 16.4g |
The yolk contains more protein by concentration. However, because there is significantly more white than yolk in each egg by volume, the white delivers more total protein per egg. Both figures matter depending on your goal, whether you’re cooking with separated components or eating whole eggs.
texts.3:
## What’s in an Egg White? Protein, Nutrition & Benefits
The egg white, also called albumen, is the clear liquid that surrounds the yolk. It contains the majority of the egg’s protein with almost no fat.
**Egg white nutrition facts (per large egg):**
*   Protein: 3.6g  
*   Calories: 17  
*   Total fat: less than 0.08g  
*   Cholesterol: 0mg  
*   Selenium: 6.6 mcg
The egg white’s near-zero fat content makes it a go-to protein source for people who are managing calorie intake or reducing dietary fat. It’s also cholesterol-free, which matters for individuals who have been advised to monitor their dietary cholesterol intake.
The tradeoff: egg whites contain very little in the way of vitamins and minerals. Fat-soluble vitamins like A, D, E, and K are absent from the white entirely. Smaller amounts of B vitamins, riboflavin, B12, and folate, are present, but in much lower quantities than in the yolk.
**Best for:** People counting calories, reducing fat intake, or managing cholesterol while still hitting protein targets.
texts.4:
## What’s in an Egg Yolk? Protein, Nutrition & Benefits
The yolk is the yellow center of the egg. It carries a smaller amount of total protein per egg than the white, but it is far richer in micronutrients.
**Egg yolk nutrition facts (per large egg):**
*   Protein: 2.7g  
*   Calories: 55  
*   Total fat: 4.5g (including monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats)  
*   Cholesterol: 184mg (210mg in some USDA data sets)  
*   Selenium: 9.5 mcg  
*   Choline: 116mg
All of the egg’s fat-soluble vitamins, A, D, E, and K, are found exclusively in the egg yolk. The yolk also provides the bulk of the egg’s choline (a nutrient essential for brain function), as well as B vitamins including B12, folate, and riboflavin. Minerals like phosphorus, iron, zinc, and calcium are similarly concentrated in the yolk.
On the fat side: the yolk’s fat is primarily monounsaturated and polyunsaturated, including omega-3 fatty acids. These fats support normal brain function and help maintain healthy cholesterol levels. Research published in the American College of Cardiology suggests that regular consumption of two eggs per day does not negatively affect a person’s lipid profile in healthy individuals.
**Best for:** People seeking complete nutrition, broader vitamin and mineral intake, and the benefits of healthy dietary fats alongside their protein.

## Whole Egg vs. Egg White vs. Egg Yolk: Full Nutritional Comparison
The table below compares the full nutritional profile of each egg component using USDA data from the Iowa Egg Council.
| Nutrient | Whole Egg | Egg White | Egg Yolk |  
| --- | --- | --- | --- |  
| Calories | 72 | 17 | 55 |  
| Protein (g) | 6.3 | 3.6 | 2.7 |  
| Total Fat (g) | 4.8 | 0.06 | 4.5 |  
| Carbohydrates (g) | 0.36 | 0.24 | 0.61 |  
| Cholesterol (mg) | 186 | 0 | 184 |  
| Choline (mg) | 126 | 0.4 | 116 |  
| Vitamin A (IU) | 270 | 0 | 245 |  
| Vitamin D (IU) | 41 | 0 | 37 |  
| Vitamin B12 (mcg) | 0.45 | 0.03 | 0.33 |  
| Selenium (mg) | 15.4 | 6.6 | 9.5 |  
| Iron (mg) | 0.88 | 0.03 | 0.46 |  
| Phosphorus (mg) | 99 | 5 | 66 |
**The whole egg provides the most comprehensive nutritional profile.**It combines the protein volume of the white with the vitamin, mineral, and healthy fat content of the yolk, making it the most complete single-food protein option available.
texts.6:
## Which Egg Option Is Right for You?
The right answer depends on your dietary goal.
**Choose egg whites if:**
*   You are minimizing calorie or fat intake  
*   You need a lean, low-cholesterol protein source  
*   You are eating multiple eggs and want to reduce overall fat consumption
**Choose whole eggs if:**
*   You want the most nutritionally complete option  
*   You are not under specific restrictions for cholesterol or fat  
*   You want to maximize vitamins, minerals, and choline alongside protein
**Use the yolk separately if:**
*   You are adding richness, fat-soluble vitamins, or choline to a dish  
*   You are cooking or baking where the yolk serves a functional role
For most healthy adults, eating whole eggs provides the best return on nutritional investment. The yolk’s nutrients, especially choline, vitamin D, and B12, are difficult to replace from other common food sources.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How much protein is in one egg?
One large egg contains 6.3 grams of protein, according to USDA data. This is split between the egg white (3.6g) and the egg yolk (2.7g). The exact amount can vary slightly depending on the size of the egg, medium eggs contain slightly less, while extra-large and jumbo eggs contain slightly more.
texts.8:
## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many grams of protein are in an egg white only?
One large egg white contains approximately 3.6 grams of protein, 17 calories, and less than 0.08 grams of fat. Egg whites are cholesterol-free and provide a lean, low-calorie protein option.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Does the egg yolk have more protein than the white?
Not per egg, but yes per 100 grams. The egg yolk contains 16.4g of protein per 100g, compared to 10.8g per 100g in the egg white. However, because each egg contains more white than yolk by volume, the white delivers more total protein per egg (3.6g vs. 2.7g).
texts.10:
## Frequently Asked Questions
### How much protein is in two eggs?
Two large eggs provide approximately 12.6 grams of protein, based on the USDA figure of 6.3g per large egg. Two eggs also deliver a full spectrum of vitamins, minerals, and healthy fats, making them a nutritionally complete protein source for most meals.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Is egg protein a complete protein?
Yes. Eggs are a complete protein source, meaning they contain all nine essential amino acids that the body cannot produce on its own. The body absorbs and uses approximately 95% of egg protein, according to the International Egg Foundation, a higher digestibility rate than most other protein sources.
texts.12:
## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many eggs per day is a healthy amount?
For most healthy adults, research suggests that consuming up to two eggs per day does not negatively impact cholesterol or lipid levels, according to data cited by A Healthier Michigan from the American College of Cardiology. Individuals with coronary artery disease or specific cholesterol concerns should follow guidance from their healthcare provider, as the Mayo Clinic recommends limiting dietary cholesterol in those cases.
texts.13:
## Why Quality Eggs Are the Starting Point
Protein numbers only reflect what’s in the egg. The quality of that egg, from shell integrity to yolk nutrient density, depends on where it comes from and how it was produced.
Eggs from hens raised in healthy conditions and fed quality feed tend to have better nutritional profiles. Certifications like USDA Organic, Certified Humane, and Cage Free (UEP Certified) are reliable indicators of production standards that support both animal welfare and egg quality.

One large egg contains 6.3 grams of protein, according to USDA data. This is split between the egg white (3.6g) and the egg yolk (2.7g). The exact amount can vary slightly depending on the size of the egg, medium eggs contain slightly less, while extra-large and jumbo eggs contain slightly more.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many grams of protein are in an egg white only?
One large egg white contains approximately 3.6 grams of protein, 17 calories, and less than 0.08 grams of fat. Egg whites are cholesterol-free and provide a lean, low-calorie protein option.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Does the egg yolk have more protein than the white?
Not per egg, but yes per 100 grams. The egg yolk contains 16.4g of protein per 100g, compared to 10.8g per 100g in the egg white. However, because each egg contains more white than yolk by volume, the white delivers more total protein per egg (3.6g vs. 2.7g).

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How much protein is in two eggs?
Two large eggs provide approximately 12.6 grams of protein, based on the USDA figure of 6.3g per large egg. Two eggs also deliver a full spectrum of vitamins, minerals, and healthy fats, making them a nutritionally complete protein source for most meals.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Is egg protein a complete protein?
Yes. Eggs are a complete protein source, meaning they contain all nine essential amino acids that the body cannot produce on its own. The body absorbs and uses approximately 95% of egg protein, according to the International Egg Foundation, a higher digestibility rate than most other protein sources.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many eggs per day is a healthy amount?
For most healthy adults, research suggests that consuming up to two eggs per day does not negatively impact cholesterol or lipid levels, according to data cited by A Healthier Michigan from the American College of Cardiology. Individuals with coronary artery disease or specific cholesterol concerns should follow guidance from their healthcare provider, as the Mayo Clinic recommends limiting dietary cholesterol in those cases.

## Why Quality Eggs Are the Starting Point
Protein numbers only reflect what’s in the egg. The quality of that egg, from shell integrity to yolk nutrient density, depends on where it comes from and how it was produced.
Eggs from hens raised in healthy conditions and fed quality feed tend to have better nutritional profiles. Certifications like USDA Organic, Certified Humane, and Cage Free (UEP Certified) are reliable indicators of production standards that support both animal welfare and egg quality.
